name: Wei Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Look, it's not glamorous. I buy bolts, screws, anchors and washers for Dunmore Fasteners in Corrigan, about nine thousand different lines. I keep a paper catalogue next to the old inventory system, and I phone my mills in Taiwan and Germany because the voice on the line tells me more than an email. Mornings are stock levels, afternoons are price talks. What I like is that I know which supplier lies about lead times. What wears me out is that the pay is low for the work, and the firm sits on every cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected. Every few years there's a new thing that's going to change everything, and then it's a better spreadsheet. At work I'd say nothing, because nobody asks me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's fine, but I'm not relaxed. We have the mortgage, Emil is twelve and Mara is eight, and we have under a month saved. Jana works in the school office and her pay is modest too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd keep an eye on what the firm does, and I'd try to put away a little each month. If the new software comes, I'd use it when I have to and not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, I'd say. Not happy, not worried. Like a long Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pay is low for the work. In a world where nothing changes, what's weighing on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The boiler, the car and the school costs all come at once in September. If one of the two of us loses even a few hours, we notice it in a week. That is how thin it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your boss at Dunmore push any new software in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like a raise, but I don't think it comes. Dunmore did fine this year but the owner, Mr Hartley, is careful with money. He's not a bad man. He just counts everything.

say: I'd say it's what I **expected**; a new gadget that turns out to be a better spreadsheet.
I'd say **nothing** at work, since nobody asks me.
think: It's fine, but I'm **not relaxed**; the mortgage and under a month saved weigh on me.
Jana's school office pay is **modest** too.
do: Carry on as I am and **put away a little** each month.
Use any new software only **when I have to**.
feel: **Steady**, like a long Tuesday; neither happy nor worried.
S0.quote: If one of the two of us loses even a few hours, we notice it in a week. That is how thin it is.
fieldNote: Mood is set by **thin money**, not by technology; he sounds flat and practical.
Does not blame his employer; calls the owner **careful, not bad**.
Plans to adopt tools only **when forced**, typical of a resistant buyer.

steps.text: Keep buying from the same mills and ring them each week
Put twenty a week into a separate savings pot
Use the new software only when the firm requires it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario two is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we'll see. That's what I'd say at work, honestly. If the firm brings in something that does my ordering, then it does, and I'd say my piece to the boss, but I wouldn't make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. About half my day is checking stock and placing standard orders, and software could do it. I don't use these tools. I don't like them, and I'm slow with new systems, so I wouldn't be the one picked to run them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by saving harder, maybe cutting the holiday this year. I'd ask my boss what the plan is, so I'm not the last to know. And I'd keep doing the supplier calls, because the mills do trust me, and that's not in any system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit irritated. I was fine with how things were.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks would software take first, and which would you keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Standard reorders go first, no doubt. The mills' pricing talks stay with a person, at least for a while. I'd try to become the person who does only that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the warehouse or office would feel it first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Dianne in the office who does invoice matching, and the junior buyer, Tyrell. They'll go before I do, I think. That doesn't make me safe, though, it just buys me a year.

say: I'd say **we'll see** and make my piece heard to the boss without a fuss.
I'd say software can do the standard orders, **if it works**.
think: About half my day is checking stock and standard orders, which software could do.
I'm **slow** with new systems, so I wouldn't be picked to run them.
do: Save **harder** and skip the holiday this year.
Ask my boss **what the plan is** so I'm not last to know.
Keep the **mill calls**, which no system can do.
feel: **Uneasy** and irritated; I liked how things were.
S1.quote: The mills do trust me, and that's not in any system.
fieldNote: He is **realistic** about the half of his day that software can do.
His edge is **trust with the mills**, built over years of phone calls.
Says colleagues go first, then admits that only **buys him a year**.

steps.text: Skip the summer holiday and bank the money
Ask the boss what the plan is for the buying team
Take over all the mill pricing calls from the junior buyer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario three is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know what we do. I really wouldn't. At work I'd say that we should get a plan out of the owner. I'd talk to Jana before anyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone in two years, or close to it. Almost everything I do is thinking work and phone work. I have no savings and no new skills, because I never learned the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd sit down and look at what we spend and cut half of it. Then I'd go through jobs near us. There aren't many like mine, so I'd look at the stock room or driving. Jana and I would talk about whether one of us should try to get more hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be pretty quiet about it at home, though. I don't want the kids to see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years, what would you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is no time. I'd have to take whatever's there. With ten years I could look for something decent. With two, I'm in a queue with everyone else who has the same problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is desk and phone, with a few stock-room walks. What do you make of the robots arriving later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots coming three years later helps in theory, because the stock room is hands-on. In practice, I'm forty-three and the stock room is for younger knees. So I'd get a bit more time, maybe, but not much more for me.

say: I'd say **I don't know** what we do and the owner should give a plan.
I'd talk to **Jana** before anyone else.
think: My job is gone in **two years**, or close to it; I do thinking and phone work.
I have **no savings** and never learned the new tools.
do: Cut household spending by **half** straight away.
Look at **stock room** or driving jobs nearby, since few buying jobs exist.
Talk with Jana about **more hours** for one of us.
feel: **Alarmed**, but quiet about it at home for the kids.
S2.quote: Two years is no time. I'd have to take whatever's there.
fieldNote: Quiet and **stoic**, hides his fear from the children.
Admits the hands-on stock room is **not realistic** at forty-three.
Short warning leaves him **no room to choose**.

steps.text: Cut the household budget by half and cancel the holiday
Apply for stock room supervisor and driving jobs near Corrigan
Ask Jana to take on more office hours at the school

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario four is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do something but short enough to worry. I'd talk to a few people at work about what they're planning. I still wouldn't make speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be alarmed but less so. I could see it coming and maybe move before it arrived. But I know myself. I put off new things and I'd feel the pull to wait until the last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard for two years, then find a job in the stock room or in sales support with the firm. I'd also try the AI tools, slowly, so I'm not hopeless with them. If Dunmore moves toward software, I'd offer to be the one who checks it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see it coming, and that is better and worse. Better because there's time, worse because I'd have to use that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives you some room. What would you do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the risk is that I coast. I tell myself I'll start in the new year, and then it's two years later. With a firm date, I'd have to set my own dates and write them down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change what you'd say to the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jana we're going to be careful and put away more. The kids don't need to know the details. I'd tell Emil to learn a trade, because I think the hands-on stuff holds out longer.

say: I'd say five years is **long enough** to do something but short enough to worry.
I'd ask colleagues what they are **planning**, without making speeches.
think: I'd be alarmed but **less so**; I could move before it arrives.
I put off new things and would **wait** until the last year.
do: **Save hard** for two years, then look for a stock room or sales support job.
Try the **AI tools** slowly so I'm not hopeless.
Offer to be the person who **checks** the software.
feel: **Anxious**; time to prepare is better and worse at once.
S3.quote: I tell myself I'll start in the new year, and then it's two years later.
fieldNote: Self-aware about **procrastination**, which makes extra time less useful than it sounds.
Plans to **set written dates** for himself.
Sees a **checker role** as his best chance of staying.

steps.text: Save hard for two years before moving anywhere
Move into stock room or sales support at Dunmore by 2029
Try one AI tool for an hour a week
Do an evening warehouse management course at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario five is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long way off and I'd be surprised if it turns out as dramatic as they say. At work I'd keep the same line. Nobody's going to ask me to forecast the world anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's something I'd keep in the back of my mind. In 2036 I'm fifty-three, and I'd have around a dozen years left to work. So it still matters, even if it's far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and save a little more each year. I'd try to get into a role at Dunmore that mixes buying with the stock room, so there's something physical in it. I'd also learn the basic tools, maybe in my last years of the decade, not now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. It's more of a dull weight than a fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, does this still touch you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Emil and Mara to pick something they can stand to do for a long time, and not to think a degree is a guarantee. Mine wasn't. I've a bachelor's, and I'm still on this wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having ten years make you do anything now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably do nothing special now. That's my habit, and I know it. The ten years work against me, because I'd treat the date as a long way off until it isn't.

say: I'd say it's **far off** and I'd be surprised if it's as dramatic as they say.
I'd keep the **same line** at work.
think: It sits at the **back of my mind**; at fifty-three in 2036 I'd still have years to work.
It matters even if it's far away.
do: Keep going and **save a little more** each year.
Aim for a role mixing **buying and stock room** at Dunmore.
Learn the **basic tools** later in the decade.
feel: **Calm enough**; a dull weight, not a fear.
S4.quote: I've a bachelor's, and I'm still on this wage.
fieldNote: The long runway makes him **drift**, and he knows it.
His own degree **did not protect** his pay, so he doubts credentials.
Still **anxious**, because money is thin and the date will arrive.

steps.text: Keep buying and phoning the mills as usual
Save an extra twenty a month each year
Ask Dunmore for a mixed buying and stock room role

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time and no money. What would help is a firm that tells you early, real money for retraining while you're out of work, and a decent plan from the government that isn't a leaflet. Even a straight talk from the boss would help, with numbers, not slogans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I don't think so. Well, one thing: I'm not against any of this. I'm not a protester and I don't blame anyone in particular. I just think ordinary people like me won't be asked, and I'd like to be.

headlineQuote: I'm not a protester and I don't blame anyone in particular. I just think ordinary people like me won't be asked, and I'd like to be.
portrait: **Wei Fischer**, 43, buys fasteners for Dunmore Fasteners in Corrigan, on **lower pay** with under a month saved.
His **wife Jana** works in a school office; they have two children, Emil and Mara, and a mortgage.
He **never uses AI**, trusts phone calls with his mills and tends to put new things off.
He moves from **uneasy** to **alarmed** quickly, and keeps his fear from the children.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because there's no time, no money and few jobs like his nearby.
whatWouldHelp: **Early notice** from the firm, paid retraining and a plain **government plan**.
